title: Xiangqi Lab English Core Curriculum
description: A prerequisite-aware, English-first learning path: understand the board, setup, pieces, and legal movement before training games, tactics, and comparisons.

lessons.title: What Is Xiangqi?
lessons.objective: Explain what Xiangqi is, how a game is won, what the board represents, and what the learner will study before any move is played.
lessons.hook: Before the first move, learn the battlefield that makes Xiangqi different.
lessons.analysis_focus: Identify the two armies, the 9x10 board, the river, the palaces, and the learning path.
lessons.visual_focus: Show the complete board as a sequence of seven visual explanations: battlefield, armies, generals, intersections, river and palaces, cannon geometry, and roadmap.

scenes.narration: Welcome to Xiangqi, Chinese chess. You’ll meet a battlefield where your plans truly matter from move one.
scenes.caption: Chinese chess begins
scenes.headline: Meet Xiangqi
scenes.visualInstruction: Show a top-down empty Xiangqi grid. Add a header label 'Xiangqi — Chinese Chess'. Apply a soft board-wide highlight to focus attention on the grid.

scenes.narration: You see two mirrored armies facing each other across the board: red and black, evenly matched.
scenes.caption: Mirrored armies
scenes.headline: Two Armies
scenes.visualInstruction: Render the standard starting position. Add a vertical symmetry axis line through the center. Use short arrows from front ranks on both sides pointing toward the opposing side. Add small side labels 'Red' and 'Black' near each army.

scenes.narration: Your mission is to checkmate the opposing General, giving no safe escape from continuous threat ever.
scenes.caption: Checkmate wins
scenes.headline: Win By Checkmate
scenes.visualInstruction: Highlight both Generals with glows. Draw converging red attack arrows toward the enemy General. Mark X icons on all its adjacent escape intersections to show no safe squares.

scenes.narration: You’re playing on nine files and ten ranks, with pieces standing on intersections, not inside squares.
scenes.caption: Lines, not boxes
scenes.headline: Lines And Points
scenes.visualInstruction: Show an empty grid with bolded lines. Add bracket annotations reading 'nine files' along columns and 'ten ranks' along rows. Pulse small dots at each intersection. Crosshatch square interiors lightly to contrast with the intersection points.

scenes.narration: Between you and your opponent, a river divides the sides, and each General begins within a walled palace.
scenes.caption: River and palaces
scenes.headline: River And Palaces
scenes.visualInstruction: Display the standard board. Shade the central river row and add a 'River' label. Draw thin borders around both three-by-three palace areas with 'Palace' labels. Highlight each General inside its palace.

scenes.narration: You’ll see the Cannon create distinctive line geometry, jumping a single screen to capture along straight firing lines.
scenes.caption: Cannon’s lines
scenes.headline: Cannon Geometry
scenes.visualInstruction: Arrange a Cannon, one intervening screen piece, and a target in the same file. Use a dashed line from Cannon to screen, then a solid line to the target. Add a small 'screen' label above the middle piece. Fade forbidden capture lines where no screen exists.

scenes.narration: In this course, you’ll learn the board, setup, pieces, moves, complete games, then tactics, step by step.
scenes.caption: Your roadmap
scenes.headline: Your Learning Path
scenes.visualInstruction: Show a left-to-right timeline with arrows and text boxes: 'Board' → 'Setup' → 'Pieces' → 'Moves' → 'Games' → 'Tactics'. Add a checkmark style for progression.

lessons.title: Xiangqi in 60 Seconds
lessons.objective: Give a fast, accurate orientation to the board, pieces, and goal.
lessons.hook: Can you understand the battlefield before the first pawn moves?
lessons.analysis_focus: Connect one visible move to the game’s attacking geometry.

lessons.title: A Short History of Xiangqi
lessons.objective: Give a careful, accessible history and cultural orientation without unsupported origin myths.
lessons.hook: The river and palaces are not decoration; they carry the game’s history and identity.
lessons.analysis_focus: Connect the modern board vocabulary to the long tradition of Chinese chess.
lessons.visual_focus: Keep the complete board visible as the narration explains the historical identity of Xiangqi.

lessons.title: Xiangqi vs Western Chess: Your First Five Differences
lessons.objective: Explain intersections, river, palaces, cannon capture, and flying generals.
lessons.hook: If you play chess already, these five rules will surprise you.
lessons.analysis_focus: Show how one move becomes different because Xiangqi pieces live on intersections and attack through open lines.

lessons.title: The 9×10 Point Board
lessons.objective: Teach intersections, nine files, ten ranks, and the battlefield map before showing a move.
lessons.hook: In Xiangqi, the pieces stand on points, not inside squares.
lessons.analysis_focus: Point out the nine files, ten ranks, intersections, center, and the two sides of the board.
lessons.visual_focus: Show the full board and its geometry without playing a training sequence.

lessons.title: The River and the Two Palaces
lessons.objective: Explain the river, the two palaces, palace limits, and why these regions change legal movement and attack plans.
lessons.hook: Two marked regions decide where the generals, advisors, and elephants can go.
lessons.analysis_focus: Make the river and palace boundaries visible before the learner studies tactical moves.
lessons.visual_focus: Hold the starting position and visually emphasize the river and palace regions.

lessons.title: Set Up All 32 Pieces
lessons.objective: Teach the complete 32-piece starting arrangement, mirror symmetry, and the role of each starting zone.
lessons.hook: A correct setup is the first legal move you make before the game begins.
lessons.analysis_focus: Identify every piece family and its starting relationship to the general, palace, river, and files.
lessons.visual_focus: Display all 32 pieces in their starting arrangement; do not turn the setup lesson into a game.

lessons.title: How Xiangqi Coordinates Work
lessons.objective: Teach the channel’s coordinate system so a beginner can follow every later example precisely.
lessons.hook: Once you can name two points, every Xiangqi explanation becomes easy to follow.
lessons.analysis_focus: Read files, ranks, source points, destination points, and the side of the river.
lessons.visual_focus: Keep the complete arrangement visible while coordinate points are introduced.

lessons.title: How to Read a Xiangqi Move
lessons.objective: Teach a beginner how to follow move notation and board arrows.
lessons.hook: A move is not a code once you know what to look for.
lessons.analysis_focus: Narrate the piece, route, purpose, opponent reply, and changed plan.

lessons.title: The General: The Piece You Must Never Expose
lessons.objective: Teach general movement, palace restriction, the flying-general prohibition, check, and safe defensive choices.
lessons.hook: Your strongest piece is also the most restricted: one illegal line can lose the game.
lessons.analysis_focus: Show a legal general move inside the palace, a legal reply that does not create a facing-general position, and a diagonal advisor move; explicitly distinguish the forbidden flying-general line from a legal defensive plan.

lessons.title: Advisors and Palace Defense
lessons.objective: Teach advisor movement and defensive coordination.
lessons.hook: A small diagonal move can be the wall in front of your general.
lessons.analysis_focus: Show the advisor blocking a route and why the attacker must change plans.

lessons.title: Elephants and the River
lessons.objective: Teach elephant movement, eye blocking, and river restriction.
lessons.hook: This diagonal piece can defend brilliantly but can never cross the river.
lessons.analysis_focus: Explain the elephant’s route, the blocked eye, and the defensive consequence.

lessons.title: The Horse and the Blocked Eye
lessons.objective: Teach horse movement and why it cannot jump through a blocked leg.
lessons.hook: A Xiangqi horse does not jump like a chess knight.
lessons.analysis_focus: Show the horse’s intended route, the blocking point, and how the opponent benefits from closing it.

lessons.title: Chariots and Open Files
lessons.objective: Teach chariot power and the need to clear a line.
lessons.hook: The chariot is quiet until one pawn steps out of its way.
lessons.analysis_focus: Explain the pawn clearance, chariot activation, enemy reply, and resulting pressure.

lessons.title: The Cannon and Its Mount
lessons.objective: Teach cannon movement, screen capture, and tactical value.
lessons.hook: The cannon attacks through a piece, not around it.
lessons.analysis_focus: Explain the cannon line, the required screen, the threatened target, and the defender’s response.

lessons.title: Soldiers Before and After the River
lessons.objective: Teach soldier movement and its changed options after crossing the river.
lessons.hook: One river crossing gives a soldier a new direction.
lessons.analysis_focus: Explain the first advance, the opponent’s reply, and what becomes available after the river.

lessons.title: Piece Combinations: Cannon, Chariot, and Horse
lessons.objective: Introduce coordination instead of isolated piece movement.
lessons.hook: Pieces become dangerous when they ask the same question together.
lessons.analysis_focus: Explain how each move improves a partner piece and limits the opponent’s reply.

lessons.title: Can You Spot the Legal Move?
lessons.objective: Review all seven piece families through a quick legal-move test.
lessons.hook: One of these moves is legal. Can you find it before the reveal?
lessons.analysis_focus: State the rule, explain the tempting illegal move, then show the legal alternative.

lessons.title: Your First Ten Xiangqi Moves
lessons.objective: Give a beginner a safe development sequence without rote memorization.
lessons.hook: Your first ten moves should develop a plan, not chase a pawn.
lessons.analysis_focus: For each move, explain development goal, opponent reply, and what line becomes safer or stronger.

lessons.title: How to Keep Your General Safe
lessons.objective: Teach early safety and direct-line danger.
lessons.hook: A good opening can fail if one file points at your general.
lessons.analysis_focus: Connect a defensive move to the enemy’s line and the response it prevents.

lessons.title: When to Develop Your Cannons
lessons.objective: Teach timing, support, and risk in early cannon development.
lessons.hook: A cannon can create pressure early, or become the target.
lessons.analysis_focus: Explain the development square, the defender’s natural reaction, and why support matters.

lessons.title: Why Chariots Need Open Lines
lessons.objective: Teach clearance and chariot activation.
lessons.hook: Do not move the chariot first; make a road for it.
lessons.analysis_focus: Explain the clearance move, the chariot’s route, and the pressure that changes the defender’s plan.

lessons.title: Play Your First Mini-Game
lessons.objective: Apply basic movement and safety in a simplified game.
lessons.hook: Before a full game, learn how a small army creates a real threat.
lessons.analysis_focus: Treat each move as a conversation: plan, response, changed target, and next plan.

lessons.title: Your First Complete Beginner Game
lessons.objective: Walk through a coherent full-game story from setup to finish.
lessons.hook: You know the pieces. Now see why a game has phases.
lessons.analysis_focus: Narrate plans and responses, not a list of moves; identify opening, turning point, and conversion.

lessons.title: Three Xiangqi Opening Principles
lessons.objective: Teach development, line opening, and general safety.
lessons.hook: A good opening has three jobs before any tactic appears.
lessons.analysis_focus: Tie every shown move to one opening principle and the opponent’s counter-plan.

lessons.title: Develop the Central Cannon
lessons.objective: Teach central-cannon purpose and early risks.
lessons.hook: The central cannon is not a ritual; it is a question for your opponent.
lessons.analysis_focus: Explain target squares, screen logic, reply options, and how center pressure changes piece development.

lessons.title: Activate the Chariot
lessons.objective: Teach when a rook/chariot joins the opening.
lessons.hook: The strongest line piece is useless behind its own pawn.
lessons.analysis_focus: Explain clearance, activation, the defender’s reply, and the file now under pressure.

lessons.title: Central Pressure Without Memorizing Lines
lessons.objective: Teach central influence as a plan rather than memorized theory.
lessons.hook: The center matters because it gives your heavy pieces choices.
lessons.analysis_focus: Describe how each move asks a central question and how the reply changes the next route.

lessons.title: The Cost of Moving the Same Piece Twice
lessons.objective: Teach tempo and development discipline.
lessons.hook: One extra move can let your opponent finish a whole plan.
lessons.analysis_focus: Compare the tempting repeat move with the opponent’s developing reply and lost time.

lessons.title: The First Beginner Opening Trap
lessons.objective: Teach a safe early tactical pattern and defense.
lessons.hook: The trap works only because one defender forgets a line.
lessons.analysis_focus: Explain bait, natural reply, tactical consequence, and the defensive alternative.

lessons.title: What Is a Forcing Move?
lessons.objective: Teach checks, captures, and threats as a calculation order.
lessons.hook: The best move often leaves the opponent the fewest useful answers.
lessons.analysis_focus: Explain the threat, enumerate the response type, and show why the reply changes the position.

lessons.title: Checks, Captures, and Threats
lessons.objective: Teach a repeatable move-search routine.
lessons.hook: Calculate in this order before you guess.
lessons.analysis_focus: State the immediate threat, the defensive reply, and the follow-up that makes the sequence work.

lessons.title: The Cannon Screen Tactic
lessons.objective: Teach how one intervening piece enables a cannon capture.
lessons.hook: The piece between the cannon and target is the whole tactic.
lessons.analysis_focus: Identify screen, target, defender reply, and why removing or adding a screen changes everything.

lessons.title: The Horse Eye Tactic
lessons.objective: Teach attack and defense through the horse-leg block.
lessons.hook: You do not capture the horse; sometimes you capture its eye.
lessons.analysis_focus: Explain the intended horse route, the blocking reply, and the strategic consequence.

lessons.title: The Flying General Rule
lessons.objective: Teach the direct-facing-generals rule and its tactical force.
lessons.hook: One open file can make a position illegal immediately.
lessons.analysis_focus: Explain the open line, the required response, and how pins arise from the general rule.

lessons.title: The Pinned Line to the General
lessons.objective: Teach line pins and overloads near the palace.
lessons.hook: A piece can look defended until moving it loses the general.
lessons.analysis_focus: Describe the pin, natural defender move, why it fails, and the clean alternative.

lessons.title: Bronze Puzzle 01: Find the Check
lessons.objective: Apply the forcing-move routine in one short puzzle.
lessons.hook: Pause now. What is the only forcing check?
lessons.analysis_focus: Give think time, then explain the threat, reply, and teaching point in natural language.

lessons.title: Bronze Puzzle 02: Open the File
lessons.objective: Use clearance to create a line attack.
lessons.hook: The winning move does not attack the general directly.
lessons.analysis_focus: Explain clearance, forced defense, and the line revealed afterwards.

lessons.title: Silver Puzzle 01: The Cannon Reply
lessons.objective: Calculate a cannon-based reply beyond the first move.
lessons.hook: The obvious capture loses. What response keeps the pressure?
lessons.analysis_focus: Explain the opponent’s threat, the counter-move, and why the screen changes the exchange.

lessons.title: Silver Puzzle 02: Save the Horse
lessons.objective: Use a tempo move to solve a horse-eye problem.
lessons.hook: Can you save the horse and create a threat at the same time?
lessons.analysis_focus: Explain the blocked route, opponent reply, and dual-purpose continuation.

lessons.title: Gold Puzzle 01: Palace Pressure
lessons.objective: Calculate a multi-move palace attack.
lessons.hook: The general has only one safe square. Can you see why?
lessons.analysis_focus: Track the escape squares, forced reply, and final net.

lessons.title: Gold Puzzle 02: The Chariot Route
lessons.objective: Find a chariot line that turns pressure into a concrete threat.
lessons.hook: The chariot needs one route, but which route cannot be stopped?
lessons.analysis_focus: Explain route selection, defender priority, and tactical payoff.

lessons.title: Master Puzzle: The Last Piece
lessons.objective: Combine line calculation, tempo, and palace awareness.
lessons.hook: One quiet move makes every defense fail.
lessons.analysis_focus: Explain why direct moves fail, why the quiet move works, and the forced response.

lessons.title: Open Lines Before Attacking
lessons.objective: Teach preparation before an attack.
lessons.hook: Do not attack a closed palace; open the route first.
lessons.analysis_focus: Explain the preparatory move, defender’s response, and how the opened file changes the attack.

lessons.title: Cannon and Chariot Coordination
lessons.objective: Teach heavy-piece cooperation.
lessons.hook: A cannon asks the question; a chariot makes the answer painful.
lessons.analysis_focus: Narrate how one piece fixes a defender and the other exploits the line.

lessons.title: When Material Is Not Enough
lessons.objective: Teach initiative, king safety, and activity beyond piece counting.
lessons.hook: Being ahead a pawn means little if your general cannot breathe.
lessons.analysis_focus: Explain how a move gains activity, forces a reply, and changes material evaluation.

lessons.title: Attack the Palace, Not the Pawn
lessons.objective: Teach target selection in the middlegame.
lessons.hook: The loose pawn is tempting, but the palace is the real target.
lessons.analysis_focus: Compare the greedy move with the palace attack, the opponent’s response, and the lasting pressure.

lessons.title: When to Switch from Attack to Defense
lessons.objective: Teach recognition of a changed position.
lessons.hook: The best attack ends when the opponent gets a counter-threat.
lessons.analysis_focus: Explain the original plan, opponent resource, defensive reply, and new strategic goal.

lessons.title: General and Soldier Endgames
lessons.objective: Teach basic promotion-side pressure and general placement.
lessons.hook: A single soldier becomes dangerous only when the general helps it.
lessons.analysis_focus: Explain advance, defender king response, and how the next square changes the result.

lessons.title: Chariot Endgame Basics
lessons.objective: Teach active chariot placement and checking distance.
lessons.hook: In a chariot ending, activity often matters before material.
lessons.analysis_focus: Explain active file, enemy general reply, and why the chariot keeps checking distance.

lessons.title: Cannon Endgame Patterns
lessons.objective: Teach why cannon value changes with available screens.
lessons.hook: A cannon without a screen is a different piece.
lessons.analysis_focus: Explain screen availability, defender reply, and when the cannon should change roles.

lessons.title: How to Recognize a Draw
lessons.objective: Teach practical draw recognition and rule-sensitive cautions.
lessons.hook: More material does not always mean a win.
lessons.analysis_focus: Explain why the active side cannot make progress, what the defender threatens, and when rules must be checked.

lessons.title: A Full Game Built Around a Cannon
lessons.objective: Show a game narrative with opening, middlegame, and conversion.
lessons.hook: This whole game begins with one cannon question.
lessons.analysis_focus: For each critical move, state plan, reply, tactical effect, and phase transition.

lessons.title: The Chariot Breakthrough
lessons.objective: Show how a file breakthrough changes a full game.
lessons.hook: The breakthrough is prepared long before the chariot moves.
lessons.analysis_focus: Explain preparation, forced response, breakthrough, and resulting endgame.

lessons.title: The Quiet Defensive Masterpiece
lessons.objective: Teach defense as active plan-making.
lessons.hook: The best move does not attack; it removes every attack.
lessons.analysis_focus: State the incoming threat, quiet defense, attacker response, and how initiative disappears.

lessons.title: Pause Before Every Critical Move
lessons.objective: Teach analysis habits during a complete game.
lessons.hook: Before the critical move, stop and calculate with me.
lessons.analysis_focus: Invite prediction, then explain candidate move, opponent reply, and calculation result.

lessons.title: The Triple-Check Motif
lessons.objective: Introduce multiple-line check patterns responsibly.
lessons.hook: In Xiangqi, more than two checking lines can appear at once.
lessons.analysis_focus: Explain every checking line, forced defense, and the position’s legal constraints.

lessons.title: Sacrifice to Open the Palace
lessons.objective: Teach when a material sacrifice opens decisive access.
lessons.hook: The sacrifice is not for material; it is for the palace door.
lessons.analysis_focus: Explain sacrifice target, forced recapture or refusal, and opened route to the general.

lessons.title: Repetition and Perpetual Check
lessons.objective: Introduce rule-sensitive repetition concepts and direct viewers to official rules.
lessons.hook: Repeated checks are not just a drawing tool; tournament rules matter.
lessons.analysis_focus: Describe the repeated threat, defender choices, and why the applicable rule set must be named.

lessons.title: Chasing Rules Explained
lessons.objective: Introduce long-chase caution with a rule-reference disclaimer.
lessons.hook: A repeated attack can be illegal depending on the tournament rule set.
lessons.analysis_focus: Explain the chase, the defensive options, and the need for an official-rule check.

lessons.title: Xiangqi vs Western Chess
lessons.objective: Compare board geometry, pieces, tactics, and game feel fairly.
lessons.hook: Both games use armies, but they reward different instincts.
lessons.analysis_focus: Use one shared-looking move to show why the response and tactical meaning differ.

lessons.title: Xiangqi vs Shogi
lessons.objective: Compare capture consequences, board structures, and tactical priorities.
lessons.hook: One game reuses captured pieces; the other makes files and cannons decisive.
lessons.analysis_focus: Compare the same planning question and how Xiangqi’s line pieces answer it.

lessons.title: Xiangqi vs Janggi
lessons.objective: Compare related traditions without flattening their rule differences.
lessons.hook: These boards look related, but their tactical language is not identical.
lessons.analysis_focus: Identify a visual similarity, then explain the strategic difference in a concrete line.

lessons.title: Xiangqi vs Go
lessons.objective: Compare direct-piece tactics with territory and influence.
lessons.hook: One game attacks a general; the other surrounds space.
lessons.analysis_focus: Use pressure and line control to explain different forms of initiative.

lessons.title: Which Board Game Rewards Calculation?
lessons.objective: Frame different games by decision style rather than superiority.
lessons.hook: Calculation means something different when the board itself changes the question.
lessons.analysis_focus: Compare forcing lines, reply space, and strategic evaluation respectfully.

lessons.title: Solve the Viewers’ Positions
lessons.objective: Create a future community-review format with consent and anonymized positions.
lessons.hook: What would you play if this were your game?
lessons.analysis_focus: Explain the viewer’s threat, candidate response, opponent resource, and teaching takeaway.

lessons.title: Beginner Game Review: Find the Turning Point
lessons.objective: Teach review habits through an anonymized beginner-style game.
lessons.hook: The game was not lost on the last move; it changed here.
lessons.analysis_focus: State the plan before the error, opponent’s reply, and a usable replacement plan.

lessons.title: Engine or Human? How to Analyze a Xiangqi Position
lessons.objective: Teach engine-assisted analysis with human explanation and verification.
lessons.hook: An engine can find a move; it cannot replace the reason you learn it.
lessons.analysis_focus: Explain candidate move, human plan, engine check, and the practical meaning for a learner.

lessons.title: The Central Cannon Pattern
lessons.objective: Consolidate a recurring central-cannon strategic pattern.
lessons.hook: The central cannon is a pattern, not one opening move.
lessons.analysis_focus: Explain the pattern’s trigger, defender reaction, and alternate plan if the line closes.

lessons.title: Palace Net Patterns
lessons.objective: Recognize repeated attack geometry around the palace.
lessons.hook: The net is built before the final check appears.
lessons.analysis_focus: Track escape squares, defender movement, and why the final move has no safe reply.

lessons.title: The Last-Piece Puzzle
lessons.objective: Test complete-pattern recognition in one compact challenge.
lessons.hook: Only one piece can move. Can it change the whole position?
lessons.analysis_focus: Give think time, then explain move purpose, forced answer, and final board effect.

lessons.title: Play and Analyze a Full Xiangqi Game
lessons.objective: Graduate by combining rules, plans, tactics, endgame awareness, and self-review.
lessons.hook: You are ready to play a full game and explain your decisions.
lessons.analysis_focus: Treat the game as a continuous dialogue: objective, opponent reply, changed position, and revised plan.
